name: Sludge
description: Friction, excessive paperwork, or other choice-architecture features that make it needlessly difficult for people to take an action that serves their own interest -- unenrolling from a subscription, claiming a benefit, canceling a service -- the deliberate or negligent opposite of a helpful nudge.
design_relevance_note: Directly names the mechanism behind cancellation flows, unsubscribe processes, benefit-claim forms, and account-deletion journeys that are made slower or more confusing than the equivalent sign-up flow -- a specific, nameable target for design-ethics review and regulatory scrutiny (e.g. the FTC's 'click-to-cancel' rulemaking).
prevalence_note: Increasingly common and specifically named in design-ethics, policy, and dark-patterns discourse (including active FTC rulemaking on subscription cancellation), though 'sludge' as a term is still newer and less universally known among practitioners than 'dark pattern' itself.

findings.description: Coins and defines 'sludge' as the harmful counterpart to a beneficial nudge: friction, excessive paperwork, or other choice-architecture features that make it needlessly difficult for people to take an action that serves their own interest (e.g., unenrolling from a program, obtaining a benefit) -- as distinct from 'nudging for evil' generally, and positioned as something a conscientious choice architect should actively remove rather than add.

Proposes that institutions (firms, government agencies) should regularly conduct 'Sludge Audits' -- a systematic accounting of the frictions/administrative burdens their processes impose on consumers, employees, or citizens -- arguing that because of behavioral biases and cognitive scarcity, sludge's true costs are typically far larger, and its incidence far more concentrated on vulnerable populations, than institutions anticipate without deliberately measuring it.

applications.title: UK regulator (CMA) investigating hotel-booking sites for commission-based rankings disguised as 'top picks' and pressure-selling messages
applications.description: The UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) launched a formal investigation into major hotel-booking sites, examining whether search results were ranked by the commission a hotel pays the platform rather than consumer-relevant factors like price or rating -- while being displayed non-transparently as objective 'top picks' -- and whether urgency/pressure-selling messages (e.g. 'X people are looking at this room') were misleading consumers about genuine scarcity or demand.
applications.ethical_note: A textbook case of Thaler's 'sludge' definition in action: friction and misdirection that discourage a consumer from making the deal-comparison decision they would otherwise make, dressed up as helpful curation ('top picks') and urgency (scarcity messaging) -- serious enough to draw a formal government regulatory investigation, not merely a debatable growth-hacking tactic.
